title: Choosing between Weekend Fostering and Independent Visiting
excerpt: Choosing between becoming an Independent Visitor and becoming a Weekender is not really about picking the “better” route. It is about finding the way of showing up for children in care that fits your…
html:
Choosing between becoming an Independent Visitor and becoming a Weekender is not really about picking the “better” route. It is about finding the way of showing up for children in care that fits your life, your home and your emotional bandwidth.

At Now Foster we meet people who:

  • start as Independent Visitors before they ever consider fostering;
  • volunteer as Independent Visitors and then become Weekenders;
  • do both at the same time; and
  • have never volunteered before but know that weekend fostering is the right first step for them.

This blog is to help you understand what each role involves, where they overlap and some questions that might help you work out which path feels right for you right now.

What is an Independent Visitor?

Independent Visitors (often called IVs) are trained volunteers who build long term, one-to-one relationships with children and young people in care.

They are:

  • independent from social services;
  • not paid professionals (but receive volunteer expenses); and
  • there purely as a consistent, trusted adult who will stick around.

An Independent Visitor usually spends a few hours with a child or young person once a month. What you do together is up to you both: playing football in the park, a museum trip, lunch in town, a bike ride or just chatting over hot chocolate.

Independent Visitor schemes are run by different organisations in different parts of England. They match volunteers with children in care and provide training, supervision and ongoing support. In London, you can become an IV with Coram Voice or with Action for Children. If you live elsewhere, you can find your local provider here.

Becoming an Independent Visitor usually involves a home visit, online training and some e-learning modules, and then a careful matching process with a young person.

For the child, the magic of an IV is simple: one adult who is there for them, who is not paid to be there, who shows up regularly and sticks to their word.

What is a Weekender?

Weekenders is Now Foster’s programme delivered in partnership with Local Authorities across London. As a Weekender you are an approved foster carer who welcomes the same child or young person into your home regularly, usually one weekend a month.

You:

  • have a spare room in your home for the child or young person
  • go through full fostering assessment and training
  • are matched with a child in care through our partner local authorities
  • receive a fostering allowance so you can cover costs and do fun things together

We often describe the role as feeling a bit more like being an involved auntie, uncle or godparent figure than a full time foster parent. Your job is to offer stability, warmth and fun, and to help the young person try new things, build confidence and create good memories. You become part of the young person’s care plan, and you help strengthen the goals that the team around the child are working towards.

Weekenders is currently running across Greater London, North Somerset and Durham.

Similarities: what IVs and Weekenders have in common

Although one is volunteering and the other is fostering, the heart of the role is surprisingly similar.

1. It is all about long term relationships
- Both IVs and Weekenders are there to build a relationship over years, not weeks. Independent Visitors commit to two years, although you can stay involved until a young person is 18, and beyond, if everyone agrees.
- Weekenders are matched with a child so that the relationship can grow over time, month by month, and we encourage everyone to consider this a long-term role, ideally until the child reaches 18 and ideally the relationship would endure beyond.

2. Children in care are at the centre
- In both roles you are there for one child or young person in care. You are the adult who remembers their favourite food, celebrates their wins and keeps turning up even when life around them is changing.

3. Quality time, not fancy activities
- Cinema trips, swimming or days out can be brilliant, but often the most important moments are the small ones: being on the sidelines at football, cooking together, or chatting on the bus home. IVs and Weekenders both focus on ordinary experiences that become extraordinary because they are consistent.

4. Training and support are provided
- Neither role expects you to arrive fully “ready”. IV providers offer training and ongoing supervision. As a Weekender you receive fostering preparation, assessment and ongoing support from your supervising social worker.

Key differences: volunteering and fostering are not the same

Here are some of the big differences people often want to understand.

Because of these differences, the “right” path will depend a lot on your current life set up.

Real journeys: how people move between the two

When we speak to prospective carers, we see a few common patterns.

“I started as an Independent Visitor”

Some people are curious about fostering but want to start with something flexible that fits around work and family life. Independent Visiting lets them:

  • understand a bit more about the care system
  • learn how it feels to build a relationship with a young person in care
  • discover what they find stretching, joyful or surprising

Later, some of those people choose to apply to become Weekenders or foster carers. They arrive with a deeper sense of why stability matters, because they have already seen it from a young person’s perspective.

“I knew I was ready to foster, but full-time felt too big a jump”

Others have never been an Independent Visitor but feel very clear that they want to foster. For them, Weekenders is a way to:

  • step into the foster carer role in a structured, supported way
  • balance caring with work or other responsibilities
  • shape their home life around a regular weekend rhythm

Some of these carers later go on to full-time fostering, and this is the perfect way to get started and build their skills. Others stay as Weekenders because it fits their life and motivation.

“I do both”

There are people who volunteer as IVs and foster at the same time, carefully managing the boundaries and time commitments with support from both schemes. Sometimes this looks like:

  • being an IV in an area where Weekenders is not yet running
  • becoming a Weekender and continuing an existing IV relationship until it naturally comes to an end

It is not about collecting roles. It is about asking, “Where can I be consistent and useful, without stretching myself too thin?”

Questions to help you decide

Here are some reflections that might help you work out what is right for you just now.

  1. Do you have a spare room and the ability to welcome a child overnight?
  • If not, Independent Visiting may be a good starting point.
  • If yes, Weekenders could be an option, or you may still prefer to begin as an IV.

2. Where do you live?

  • If you are in Greater London, North Somerset or Durham, you may be able to apply to be a Weekender with us.
  • If you are elsewhere in the UK, an IV scheme might be the quickest way to get involved while we grow Weekenders into more areas.

3. Are you willing to commit to an in-depth assessment

  • Becoming a Weekender involves going through the full fostering assessment, and ensuring your house is safe for the child. You also need to maintain and update your registration with an annual review each year. You can find more information about the whole process here.
  • The process to become an IV is more light touch because your home environment does not need to be assessed in depth, so this may be better if you have less availability.

4. What does your typical month look like?

  • Could you reliably commit one weekend a month to caring, alongside some meetings and training?
  • Or would a few hours on a weekday evening or Saturday afternoon be more sustainable?

5. How ready do you feel for the responsibilities of fostering?

  • Weekending involves being part of a professional network around a child, including being part of the care plan.
  • IVs focus more on relationship and advocacy from the outside, with less formal responsibility for day-to-day care, and less involvement in any decisions relating to the care of the child.

6. What length of commitment can you offer?

  • If you think you may not be able to do more than 2–3 years, IV is a better choice for you
  • If you think that you can see yourself committed for the next 4–5 years, you can explore Weekenders but consider a match with an older child who might need you less in five years time.
  • If you want to be around for the long-term, then being a Weekender for a younger child could be a great fit!

7. What kind of support do you want or need?

  • Both roles offer training and supervision, but fostering support can feel more intensive, which some people really value.

And remember, there is no rule that says you must do one before the other. This is not a linear ladder. It is more like a set of paths that you can move between as your life and circumstances change.

What to do next

If you are feeling drawn towards becoming an Independent Visitor:

  • You can read more about what IVs do and how to apply on the IV Network website.
  • Your local authority may also be able to signpost you to your nearest IV scheme.

If you are curious about becoming a Weekender:

  • Visit the Weekenders section of our website to learn more about what the role involves, what support you receive and who we are currently recruiting in partnership with.

Wherever you are starting from, you do not have to figure it out alone. If you are weighing up Independent Visiting, Weekenders or another route entirely, you are very welcome to get in touch with Now Foster. We can talk through your situation, your questions and your hopes for the future, and work out together what a meaningful next step could look like for you and for a young person in care!

title: Is now the right time to be a Weekender?
excerpt: There’s no perfect moment to step into a child’s life. But some moments are easier than others. Our team have put together a guide to help you reflect on your own circumstances.
html:
There’s no perfect moment to step into a child’s life. But some moments are easier than others. Our team have put together a guide to help you reflect on your own circumstances.

If you’ve been thinking about becoming a weekend foster carer, you might be wondering: is now the right time? It’s a good question, and an important one! Because while the desire to help matters, so does timing. Your circumstances matter. Not just for your wellbeing, but for the child’s too.

The Weekenders programme is built around long-term relationships. Many of the children and young people we support haven’t had much consistency in their lives, and our aim is to change that. We want to give you the best possible chance to be that steady, supportive presence over time. (You can read what that looks like in practice through a real-life Weekenders story here.)

None of us can predict the future, but the ideal starting point is one where you can offer consistency during the early stages of a match. Once trust has been built, it becomes easier to navigate changes, whether in your life or in the child’s life.

What follows is a list of situations where it might not be the right moment to begin weekending. These aren’t hard rules, and they’re definitely not deal-breakers. Think of them as prompts for reflection: things to consider and talk through during your home visit.

You’re planning to move house soon

Moving house is one of life’s big upheavals. Whether it’s around the corner or across the country, the disruption to your routines, stability and mental energy can make it harder to offer consistency. If you’re in transition, give yourself permission to land first.

You’re not sure you’ll be in the country long-term

Weekending is about being a consistent adult in a child’s life. If there’s a real chance you might move abroad in the next two to five years, it could be worth waiting until you have a clearer sense of your plans.

That said, it doesn’t automatically rule you out. Your potential timeline may shape how you’re matched. For example, a fostering service may consider you as a Weekender for a teenager who’s likely to need less support by the time you leave.

You have other big life events coming up

Weddings, surgeries, new babies in the family — whatever’s ahead, big life events take time and emotional energy. That doesn’t mean you can’t start weekending during them, but it’s important to think honestly about your capacity for the assessment process and to be consistent in the early stages of the match.

You have significant unprocessed trauma

You don’t need to be “perfect” to be a weekender. Plenty of carers live with their own experiences of trauma. But if you’re still in the thick of something that hasn’t had space to be processed, especially if it’s likely to be triggered by your experience with the care system, now might not be the right moment.

You want to build a family in the future

Many people are drawn to Weekending because they want children to be part of their lives. For some, this runs alongside hopes of building a family in the future, for example through birth children, full-time fostering or adoption. If this is the case for you, it’s important to think carefully about how and when you might pursue this and how it could impact your ability to offer consistency to a Weekender child.

Weekending is a long-term commitment that requires emotional availability, reliability, and a willingness to remain a stable presence through life’s changes. While we understand that life evolves (e.g. new relationships, moves, or having children of your own) we ask that prospective Weekenders consider from the start how they will continue to prioritise the Weekender child over time.

You’re undergoing fertility treatment

It’s more common than you might think for people considering fostering to also be going through fertility treatment.

Exploring Weekending while also considering fertility treatment is a situation that requires thoughtful reflection. It doesn’t automatically exclude someone from becoming a Weekender, but it does present a more complex set of emotional and practical considerations. Applicants are encouraged to think deeply about how they might respond both emotionally and physically to fertility treatment, whether it is successful or not.

The role of a Weekender is to offer children a secure, stable, and consistent relationship, often after significant instability in their lives. It’s therefore important to consider whether this is the right time to take on such a commitment and whether it’s possible to offer a child the predictability and emotional availability they need. Ultimately, the responsibility lies with the applicant to assess their capacity to manage both journeys with clarity and sensitivity.

Your housing situation is insecure

If you’re not sure where you’ll be living in three months, it can be difficult to offer a child any sense of stability. This doesn’t mean you need to own a home or have everything sorted, but you do need to feel secure enough to show up consistently.

You’re struggling with your mental health or newly starting treatment

You absolutely don’t need to be “mentally well” in any neat or final way. But if you’re currently in the depths of mental health challenges, or just beginning to get help, it’s okay to let this be a season of receiving care, not giving it.

Your job is all-consuming

Some jobs demand our weekends, our evenings, and most of our headspace. If your work is leaving you depleted, it might not be the right time to step into something that needs presence and spaciousness. And that’s okay.

What if some of this applies to me?

It doesn’t mean you’re automatically ruled out from becoming a Weekender. It just means it’s something to explore. We can talk it through with you — gently, honestly, and without pressure.

If any of these things feel relevant to you, it helps to bring them up during your intro chat or your home visit. Some people find it easier to share over email or in person, whatever works best for you.

We’ll help you think about timing, and whether now is the right moment to get started. If it’s not, we can talk through what you might do in the meantime to prepare for fostering in the future.

title: Making time to make a difference: your time commitment before and after you become a Weekender
excerpt: If you’re thinking about becoming a Weekender foster carer, you might already know the basics: one weekend a month, sometimes school holidays if you’re up for it. Simple, right?
html:
If you’re thinking about becoming a Weekender foster carer, you might already know the basics: one weekend a month, sometimes school holidays if you’re up for it. Simple, right?

But what about everything that happens before you get to that stage — when you’re just starting to explore whether fostering is right for you? And what happens after you’re approved, in those in-between moments when you’re juggling work, family, and everything else life throws your way?

Let’s break down what the commitment really looks like, both before and after you become a Weekender with support from Now Foster.

🕓 Before You’re Approved: What Happens and When

Becoming a Weekender doesn’t happen overnight — and that’s a good thing. It’s important you feel confident, supported, and informed before you commit to building a long-term relationship with a child or young person. Here’s what the early steps look like in terms of commitment:

1. First: a home visit

Before you even formally apply, we’ll come to you. One of our Now Foster team will visit your home for a 2–3 hour chat to explore what fostering might look like for you. This is your space to ask questions, find out more, share more about your circumstances, and decide if you want to take the next step.

2. Initial Training

If you decide to go ahead, you’ll start your Weekender preparation training with Now Foster. In practice this includes one day training (at the weekend, sometimes virtually or in person in central London) and some additional evening sessions run virtually where you will top up your knowledge.

We know that it’s nice to meet people in person too, so we run different social events where you can meet other people who want to become Weekenders.

3. The Assessment Process

Once you formally apply (after home visit and training), you’ll be allocated an assessment social worker. They’ll visit you at home several times to get to know you better and understand your motivation and readiness for fostering. Some key things to know:

  • Some visits might need to happen during work hours — this will depend on your social worker’s availability.
  • Some sessions can be virtual — you can discuss this with your assessment social worker.
  • If you’re applying as a couple, there’ll be both joint and individual sessions.
  • The number of visits depends on the length of each visit and the specific details of your situation, but it tends to be between 4 and 8 visits over 2–4 months.

4. Final Step: panel

When your assessment is complete, you’ll attend a fostering panel — a group of professionals who review and formally approve your application. This is usually during the working week, and it takes an hour, so you may need to take time off work. You will know the timing months in advance, so you can arrange your schedule accordingly.

✅ After you’re approved: your ongoing commitment

Once you’re approved, you become part of a support network that’s there for you — not just when a child is staying with you, but in between, too.

1. Your Supervising Social Worker (SSW)

You’ll be allocated a dedicated SSW who will check in with you regularly. This may be more often at the beginning of your journey (e.g. every 4-6 weeks) and then less often as you settle into your role. You may also meet them more often if you need help.

Together, you’ll work out:

  • When it works best to meet — some visits can be virtual, and all of them will be planned well in advance.
  • How to keep your weekending experience supported and smooth
  • One of you (if you’re fostering as a couple) will be the “main carer” — but your SSW will want to get to know you both

2. Annual reviews & ongoing training

Each year, you’ll do a review with your SSW to reflect on your experiences and training. You’ll need to:

  • Complete some regular training (which you can often do online, through your local authority, or even use training or CPD you may be doing through work or volunteering if it’s relevant)
  • You’ll also need to complete a paediatric first aid course, normally every three years — this is in-person, and dates will depend on your fostering service.
  • Talk about how things are going, discuss any changes in your life, and explore what support you may need

Some workplaces allow time off for foster carer training (e.g. to attend your first aid course) or any key meetings. Ask your employer whether they have a HR policy for foster carers or if they are part of the national Fostering Friendly Employers scheme.

3. Professional meetings (optional but helpful)

On a regular basis, there will be meetings involving other professionals supporting the child — such as teachers or social workers. These include reviews of the child’s care plan and their education.

These meetings are:

  • Usually scheduled in advance and taking place during work hours
  • They may be virtual or in person
  • They are not mandatory for the Weekender, but if you can attend, it’s a great way to connect to the child’s wider support team

👫 Fostering as a couple? Here’s what you need to know:

  • You both need to complete training and assessment.
  • Your assessment social worker will want to get to know you together and individually.
  • After approval, only one of you needs to be at supervision meetings as the main carer — but your SSW will want to check in with both of you sometimes.

💭 Unsure about time commitment? Here’s what to keep in mind:

If you’re trying to figure out whether weekending fits into your life, here are some reflections that might help:

  • Before approval: It’s a few months of training and assessment visits, with a degree of flexibility. You’ll need to carve out a bit of time (including possibly taking some hours off work), but you will be able to plan this in advance.
  • After approval: One weekend a month with your weekender, plus a handful of check-ins, training hours, and meetings spread throughout the year.

If you don’t think you can fit in the process in your schedule, you may want to explore other opportunities to support children and young people in care, such as Independent Visiting. This is a volunteering role which does not include overnight stays, so the recruitment and support process is a bit more light-touch.

🙋 Want to Know More?

We’re always happy to talk about what fostering might look like for you. If you’re curious about timelines, training, or how weekending could work around your life, get in touch with the team — just book an intro chat in our diaries. No pressure, just a conversation that may change your life!

title: One Weekend a month could change a child’s life — and yours
excerpt: In a recent conversation on BBC Radio 4, Now Foster’s CEO, Sara Fernandez, and her foster kid, Chanice, shed light on the transformational power of weekend fostering. Their discussion revealed that…
html:
In a recent conversation on BBC Radio 4, Now Foster’s CEO, Sara Fernandez, and her foster kid, Chanice, shed light on the transformational power of weekend fostering. Their discussion revealed that becoming a Weekender can create lasting memories and opportunities for a child — while also bringing joy, purpose, and connection into your own life.

Sara and Chanice fell into the Weekender relationship by ‘accident’ over ten years ago. Now Foster is working with local authorities in Greater London to increase the number of children and young people who benefit from this support.

5 Minutes On - 'My weekend fosterer changed my life' - BBC Sounds

A Different Kind of Foster Relationship

In this radio interview, you will meet Sara and Chanice, a pair whose relationship embodies the essence of the Weekenders programme. Sara isn’t a full-time foster carer — she’s a “foster aunt,” a trusted adult who has played an important role in Chanice’s life for over a decade. Their bond proves that fostering doesn’t have to be an all-or-nothing commitment; it can be about consistency, trust, and shared experiences.

Sara recalls meeting Chanice when she was just six years old — “full of beans and up for trying new things.” Now, at almost 18, Chanice is preparing for the next chapter of her life, inspired by their shared love of theatre. From attending their first theatre show together to now choosing to pursue a career in musical theatre, Sara has been able to show Chanice possibilities she may not have otherwise considered.

The impact of Weekenders

Chanice speaks passionately about the difference having a Weekender made in her life:

“Without Sara, I wouldn’t be doing what I do today. I wouldn’t be pursuing theatre. My whole life would be completely different.”

She also highlights the reality of the care system — many children move frequently, lack stable support, and miss out on the experiences that shape a confident, independent future. Weekend foster carers can provide a stable and long-term presence in the life of a child who experiences uncertainty or instability.

About the Weekenders programme

Now Foster’s Weekenders programme works across London in partnership with local authorities to offer a new type of fostering for people who want to make a difference but cannot currently offer a full-time commitment.

For those who have been considering fostering, a Weekender role is a perfect first step. It offers insight into the fostering experience and allows individuals to learn new skills and consider whether they may be able to foster full-time in the future.

Most importantly, Weekenders is a chance to mentor, support, and help a child navigate life’s challenges, whether that’s learning to read, discovering a passion, or simply feeling understood. For Sara and Chanice, their time together has been about doing life together — cooking, watching movies, and even knitting. Simple activities that provided stability and friendship.

Could You Be a Weekender? Take the First Step

If their conversation has inspired you to learn more about becoming a Weekender, Now Foster would love to hear from you.

Visit the Now Foster’s website to find out more and take the first step toward making a difference.

title: Supporting Children in Care: Opportunities Beyond Greater London
excerpt: At Now Foster, we’re passionate about connecting people with opportunities to support children in care. While we’re currently recruiting in Greater London, we know that fostering and providing…
html:
At Now Foster, we’re passionate about connecting people with opportunities to support children in care. While we’re currently recruiting in Greater London, we know that fostering and providing support should not be limited by geography.

If you’re outside of London or don’t have a spare room but still want to make a difference, there are other ways you can get involved:

Exploring short-breaks fostering

Your local authority fostering service may recruit foster carers who offer short breaks. You may come across the idea of respite care, a type of fostering that has primarily supported full-time foster carers by giving them a break. However, some local authorities offer child-centred short breaks support, which is similar to our Weekenders programme and enables you to form a long-term relationship with a young person. This type of care focuses on providing enriching, positive experiences for children in care, rather than just supporting the primary carers or stepping in when things are not very stable. You may also come across short breaks specifically designed to support children and young people with disabilities.

We recommend reaching out to your local authority fostering service to see if they offer this type of fostering. Each area operates slightly differently, but many are open to flexible and part-time support arrangements.

Becoming an Independent Visitor

If fostering isn’t an option for you at this time, independent visiting schemes provide another meaningful way to support children in care. Independent visitors are volunteers who build long-term, trusted relationships with children and young people in care, offering friendship and guidance. While this does not typically involve overnight stays, it is a great way to make a real impact. You can find out more about independent visiting on the IV Network website.

One organisation offering this service is Coram Voice. Here’s what you need to know about becoming an independent visitor through Coram:

  • The process begins with a home visit and takes around two months to complete onboarding.
  • Once approved, the time taken to match you with a child depends on location, as well as preferences regarding age, gender, and interests.
  • Training is conducted online and consists of a four-hour session, alongside some additional e-learning modules.

You can also find more information on their website: Coram Voice — Independent Visitors. There may be a different local provider of independent visitign services in your area — get in touch with us if you need help finding it.

Looking to the Future

At Now Foster, we’re committed to expanding our programme and reaching more areas across the UK. As we grow, we hope to offer more people the chance to become Weekenders in different regions.

If you’re passionate about supporting children in care, we encourage you to explore these alternative routes while we work on expanding our reach. And if you have friends in London who may be interested in fostering, please share our programme with them!

title: “I hope it’s a lifelong relationship, and I cannot wait to see him grow up!”
excerpt: Laurie Kilby is the co-founder and Practice Lead at Now Foster. Last year she became a Weekend Foster Carer, and has been matched with a young teenage boy. They see each other regularly once per…
html:
Laurie Kilby is the co-founder and Practice Lead at Now Foster. Last year she became a Weekend Foster Carer, and has been matched with a young teenage boy. They see each other regularly once per month for the weekend, and sometimes during the school holidays.

For those who are new to Weekenders, tell us a bit about what this programme entails

Weekending is spending a minimum of 1 weekend a month with the same child or siblings. It is called Weekending because it does not signify a power imbalance in the relationship; and young people like that. You are their Weekender and they are yours.

Weekenders typically start out doing one weekend per month, but the plans can evolve and become more flexible to support the needs of the child, the full-time carer and your own family. I sometimes have my Weekender when his full-time carers want a date night and recently I’ve started having him for some school holidays too. He is just an absolute delight. I love it.

In practice, what does your Weekend fostering role look like day-to-day?

My Weekender and I laugh, saying that I am ‘all the fun, no school run’ and in many ways I am; but I am also the person who weaves in secret lessons. When my Weekender arrives on a Friday, I give him a bank card I signed him up for and he walks around the supermarket with a calculator as we plan a feast for the weekend. He thrives with the responsibility; is learning independent skills; and we bond over our shared love of stuffed crust pepperoni pizza. He literally brightens my world the second he arrives, frequently tormenting me too, but my world is better for it.

Our weekends together consist of trampolining, playing football, playing minecraft (a game I will never understand but do pretend to like), and conversations about everything from stuffed crusts to relationships. Last week he asked me about Pride month and why there isn’t a month to raise awareness for ‘kids in care’. I couldn’t answer but it did start a conversation about his identity. Friday night is Marvel film night and he always goes to bed half an hour late. I started Weekending to top him up, the reality is he tops me up, my life has considerably more meaning for him being in it.

Why did you decide to become a Weekender?

I have never wanted children of my own. I grew up in a home where my mum was a foster carer and this has single-handedly had the biggest impact on how I see the world and the role I want to play in it. I know I have so much to offer, I have built a great life, I have lots of transferable skills and I wanted to share this with my Weekender. He is someone I can consistently show up for and be there for. I hope it’s a lifelong relationship, and I cannot wait to see him grow up!

What is your advice for others going through the process?

Do it! Start it now, don’t put it off. I spent so much of my life adding to a list of ‘I will do it later’ when actually, Weekending was something I was able to do now.

The reality is, the process to become a foster carer can be hard — it takes time and emotional effort. However, the process is also really interesting. I had to look at certain aspects of myself and my past during the assessment that aren’t always easy to talk about, it was almost like therapy in reality. Now that I am where I am and it all seems a distant memory, but I can tell you it was definitely worth it.

You have a busy life! How do you make Weekend fostering work?

This works because I am busy! I look, sound and live very differently to my Weekender’s full-time carers and this benefits my Weekender. My Weekender loves talking about my life and what I have been up to and he reflects that when he is older he’s going to have a good job and help people — like I do. He knows that even in all my busy life, I choose him and I will always prioritise time with him.

Weekend Fostering is about building a lasting relationship with a child by fostering for just one weekend per month. Find out more and check if you can be a Weekender via our readiness checker.

title: Working in partnership with Local Authorities in London to support care-experienced young people
excerpt: Find out more about our funded programme to build the pipeline of foster carers across London.
html:
Find out more about our funded programme to build the pipeline of foster carers across London.

Over the past month, we have heard from 400+ people who want to become Weekend Foster Carers in London. They are motivated to support care-experienced young people, and to make a difference. They bring diverse experiences working with children, and transferable skills. The vast majority of them tell us that they see Weekend Foster Care as a stepping stone into other types of fostering in the future.

We are now looking for up to two more Local Authorities in London who would like to pioneer this programme in their service. With support for Weekenders, you can deliver a child-centred alternative to traditional respite arrangements, and boost your recruitment pipeline for future in-house foster carers.

Read on to find out more about Weekenders, and express your interest by September 2024 to participate in the funded programme.

A collaborative approach to deliver Weekenders

Now Foster works with Local Authorities to recruit and support Weekend Foster Carers, who regularly support the same child throughout their life. They become foster carers in your service, offering a long-term loving relationship that supports children to thrive.

This programme is based on a pilot in Newham in 2023–24, and research into the effects of positive lasting relationships for children in care.

Now Foster works alongside the Local Authority to build a pipeline of high quality enquiries, and delivers journey support throughout the initial stages, adding capacity to the recruitment team at the Local Authority, sharing knowledge and best practice.

Weekenders make a difference in the lives of children

We are passionate about the impact that Weekend foster carers can have by being a loving, long-term presence in the lives of care-experienced young people.

We have heard that from the care-experienced young people in our advisory board, who reflect positively on the people who offered them a loving relationship, and the potential of Weekend foster carers to do that at scale.

Weekenders look after the same child regularly. They are a safe consistent adult that moves with them throughout their life. It provides a more child-centred version of respite, which allows people to step into fostering in a way they haven’t been able to before. These foster carers bring an altruistic motivation, and are committed to learning skills that can equip them to foster more or differently in the future

We believe that with Weekend foster carers:

  • Children will have another safe adult in their life as recommended by the care review.
  • Children and young people have more holistic opportunities that they may not otherwise experience.
  • Full-time foster carers will get support, making their roles more sustainable.
  • Weekend foster carers have the potential to become tomorrow’s skilled full-time foster carers, supporting Local Authorities to build their pipeline of in-house foster carers.

With support from Weekenders, we expect to see young people leaving care ambitious for their education and careers, supported by loving adults and strong networks that will be with them for life.

About Now Foster

Now Foster is a charity that enables more people to experience the joy of fostering. We work with public sector organisations across the UK to reimagine fostering and empower brilliant foster carers to support children and young people.

Get in touch to find out more: hello (@) nowfoster.org

title: Our care-experienced advisors reflect on Weekenders
excerpt: As we get ready to launch our Weekenders programme across London, we have sought their expertise to ensure that children and young people’s voices are central to our work.
html:
As we get ready to launch our Weekenders programme across London, we have sought their expertise to ensure that children and young people’s voices are central to our work.

Our team, composed of foster carers and individuals who grew up in foster families, brings invaluable lived experience to our mission. We’re also proud to collaborate with an incredible group of care-experienced young people who provide vital insights into our programmes.

Weekenders are foster carers who commit to supporting a child long-term as they grow up. We believe this can be immensely positive for children, who will have another safe adult in their life as recommended by the care review. By recruiting Weekenders, we can also build the pipeline for future full-time foster carers.

We feel encouraged by the feedback provided by our care-experienced advisors about Weekenders, both in terms of the nature of the programme and the way it’s framed:

💬 “It’s not just another person with a notebook who writes things about me. They actually want to befriend me and have that relationship with me. We can get to know each other and maybe have similar interests. That’d be really cool.”

💬 “I think the term Weekender is cool. It’s less formal. Social worker, foster carer sounds so ‘ugh’ it’s so professional and boring. If it sounds too professional then you’ll think that this person is just temporary.”

This reflects some of the damaging experiences of a traditional use of respite care in fostering.

💬 ‘With respite care. I’m not really a fan of it because as a young person going from place to place and already feeling rejected it is more traumatising.
💬 ‘Sometimes the foster carers can’t take the children on holidays with them because there are issues with the papers or they don’t have the money. The young person is then already feeling left out and then having to go to another foster carer they don’t know will make them feel like they are not part of the family.’

Weekenders can help support children and young people in a variety of situations. We’re particularly interested in the way in which Weekenders can attract a diverse pool of foster carers. This can help support care-experienced young people living with families who are not able to meet their cultural or identity needs:

💬 ‘My foster carer was lovely, don’t get me wrong but she had religious values so to be able to talk to someone more open minded was good.’ (a care-experienced advisor about a mentor experience)
💬 ‘When I first got put into foster care I was 13 and I struggled a lot with my foster placements. The first family I was with were Ethiopian and I’m from Congo and the cultures are quite different. And they were old and I didn’t really know how to communicate with them.’

Weekenders can also support children living in kinship placements or residential settings, increasing their access to fun opportunities and strong loving relationships. We’ll be sharing more stories of Weekend foster care over the summer to highlight the ways in which the programme can make a difference.

With thanks to all the care-experienced advisors who are supporting the development of our work

Are you ready to make a difference in a child’s life? Become a Weekend Foster Carer with Now Foster. Find out more.

title: Family building through fostering and adoption — a partnership project
excerpt: Over the past few months, Coram and Now Foster collaborated on a project to explore ways to raise the profile of fostering and adoption amongst people at the beginning of their family building…
html:
Over the past few months, Coram and Now Foster collaborated on a project to explore ways to raise the profile of fostering and adoption amongst people at the beginning of their family building journey.

This blog shares some of the insight gathered from the research to date, alongside learning generated from the project. If you want to learn more about this work, get in touch! You can message us via LinkedIn Catherine Hardy at Be My Family and Sara Fernandez at Now Foster.

Our current context: two separate routes, often misunderstood.

The way that adoption and fostering are organised means that these two options are very isolated from each other. This leads to significant misunderstandings for people who are looking at their family building options. Over our test-and-learn work, we often found that people did not have a clear understanding of the differences between fostering and adoption, and in particular, there were significant misconceptions about fostering.

As part of this project, we wanted to put fostering and adoption on a more equal footing, help people understand the similarities and differences between these options, and make a decision about whether fostering or adoption would work best for them.

Developing new language and messaging.

A key way to address the misinformation challenges focused on speaking to people earlier in their journey, before they felt like they were already committed to a particular plan.

The refreshed approach tested through Be My Family focused on ‘family building’ language. The core idea was to focus on the fact that children require the same amazing additional parent regardless of whether the plan for them is fostering or adoption. We highlighted the day-to-day similarities in parenting, while clearly explaining the difference in parental responsibilities and the legal framework underpinning both.

This involved putting fostering and adoption side-by-side in a wide range of areas, such as the application process, parenting, professional support, helping potential ‘additional parents’ gain an in-depth understanding of both routes, and make their own decision.

Helping people take the next step towards family building.

We have spoken to many families and individuals in the development of this work, which have highlighted the need to continue this independent, information-focused work. It’s important to note that Be My Family does not try to advocate for one or the other, but instead focuses on educating people so that they can make their own decisions, ask questions, and most importantly, take the next step in their journey. This is essential because many people tell us they think they want to foster or adopt, but this is a very theoretical consideration. Through family building, we want to help people take practical steps towards seriously exploring fostering or adoption.

Three different households were supported through the family building route. One of them has gone on to explore adoption, one of them has expressed interest in becoming a Weekend foster carer, and one of them is still thinking about their future plans.

Reaching people earlier in their journey.

Building a family through fostering or adoption can be a very private decision, which increases the difficulty of finding people at an early stage. Most people who reach the fostering or adoption early stages have spoken to people in their immediate network who have been involved in one of those routes, but they may not have had the information to consider both family building options side-by-side. We are interested in working with employers and community groups to increase awareness amongst people who may be thinking about family building in the medium to long term.

Find out more.

Get in touch with us if you are interested in this work:

  • Visit Be My Family website to learn more about family building.
  • Help us host family building events with employers or other interest groups.
  • Get in touch if you want to put adoption and fostering side-by-side in your work.

title: Weekend fostering supports children to thrive
excerpt: The most important impact of Weekend Fostering is the value that weekenders can have for the experience of children and young people in care. They provide an additional safe adult, access to…
imageAlt: A child and an adult’s hands on a playground, helping the child balance on a log
html:
The most important impact of Weekend Fostering is the value that weekenders can have for the experience of children and young people in care. They provide an additional safe adult, access to opportunities and more people in a child’s life who can demonstrate an unconditional positive regard towards the child.

Weekend foster carers are matched for a long-term relationship, and offer a space to be relentlessly child-centred, focusing on building strengths and giving young people opportunities to succeed.

We know that there are many people who are willing to become Weekend Foster Carers, and we are excited about the potential impact that this offer can have on different types of fostering placements and situations.

We believe Weekend Foster Carers can play a role in a myriad of situations, including:

  • Supporting all children in care in long-term fostering arrangements by providing them with more safe adults. We believe in the importance of specifically matching young people to Weekend Foster Carers to meet needs which the main carer may not be able to support. For example, a trans Weekend Foster Carer supporting a teenager who identifies as gender fluid, or a Weekender supporting a child from their same cultural background.
  • Supporting kinship placements and special guardians. Weekend fostering has the potential to give connected carers the best possible support, enhancing children’s opportunities and strengthening their placement with their birth family.
  • Bringing personal relationships to those children and young people living in children’s homes. We know many children end up in homes because of a shortage of carers. A weekend fostering arrangement may be particularly important for those children who may have the potential for step-down opportunities to live in a foster family.
  • Finally, we think there is potential to explore the role that Weekend Foster Carers can play in edge of care situations. We know that creative initiatives in this space have been piloted in different local authorities. However, there is scope for further development, scale and evaluation to test the potential of this work.

Beyond the immediate impact on the child, we can also see positive benefits to existing full-time carers, who have another adult in their lives to advocate for their foster child and can help to prevent the overwhelm and burnout currently experienced by many carers. One of our hypotheses is that providing weekend support can contribute to placement stability by improving child outcomes and alleviating the pressures faced by foster families.

There are wider potential benefits to the system, which we are keen to explore through rigorous implementation and evaluation of a Weekend Fostering programme. We believe that this group of weekend carers can become a long-term pipeline of foster carers in the fostering system. They may be able to step up their involvement beyond weekends to other school holidays and arrangements that support the child. Weekend carers may be able to support in an emergency, or become a more full-time carer in the case of placement breakdowns. There are many factors that will influence whether this hypothesis holds, including the motivations of people becoming weekend foster carers, and the experience they have in their fostering service.

Regardless of whether the weekend carers step up their involvement in fostering, there is a potential tangential impact to be had from their deeper knowledge of and involvement in the fostering system. These carers may be the employers, relatives, friends or professionals in the lives of other foster carers and care-experienced young people. We believe that mainstreaming foster care involves giving more people a stake in the lives of children cared for by the local authorities.

We’re launching Weekenders across London in Spring 2024. If you want to be involved in the programme, as a Local Authority, Foster Carer, or other supporter, just get in touch with us! You can email us at hello (@) nowfoster.org
